story_intro_1:
It all began on 1 June 2169, with silence.

At 11:42, communications with the advanced research station TR-01 Huygens, on Triton, in orbit around Neptune, abruptly stopped.

No distress signal.
No alert.

The transmission was cut off in the middle of a conversation about the quality of the food rations…
story_intro_2:
We did not know it yet, but it was humanity's first encounter with an intelligent alien species.

91 people lived on Huygens station. 91 men and women, killed in the sudden destruction of their home…

In the months that followed, every human base in the outer systems was destroyed by those we would come to call the Avioids. Hundreds of thousands dead in a few weeks. The EDF (Earth Defense Force) was swept away.

No language.
No communication.
No demands.

Only attacks, and the methodical, systematic destruction of everything human.
story_intro_3:
Without Mars, the Avioids would have swept us away and humanity would no longer exist.

With the help of Grok 294.5, the superintelligence that runs the planet, Mars had built a new kind of combat ship: the EDF42-Shield fighters, which everyone simply calls Shields.

Thanks to them, and to a handful of pilots ready to die, the Avioids were held back… for a while.

But little by little, the Shields were all destroyed, one after another, by endless hordes of enemies.
story_intro_4:
Today, two years after the destruction of Huygens station, the last Shield has been destroyed and I am the only Shield pilot still alive.

I am on my way to Phobos, to a research station where, they say, a Shield prototype is still left. Professor Kamarasov uses it for his research on macroscopic quantum entanglement.

Kamarasov and Grok 294.5 have fitted the EDF-Shield-NX01 with their fabulous device: the quantum anchor. When the Shield-NX01 is destroyed, its quantum double reappears at the base, along with its pilot! Every mission makes the next one less perilous.

Hope is reborn. Aboard this prototype that can barely fly, I can turn the tide of history, I, {name}, I am now certain of it.
story_intro_4v:
Today, two years after the destruction of Huygens station, the last Shield has been destroyed and I am the only Shield pilot still alive.

I am on my way to Phobos, to a research station where a Shield prototype is still left: the EDF-Shield-NX01. Professor Kamarasov worked there on macroscopic quantum entanglement, with Grok 294.5.

But an Avioid spy drone had slipped into the station. Professor Kamarasov was killed before he could finish his invention.

The quantum anchor was never completed. If the NX01 is destroyed, it will not come back. Nor will its pilot.

There is little hope. But aboard this prototype that can barely fly, I can still turn the tide of history, I, {name}, I am now certain of it.
story_scene_dome_1:
A few survivors, escaped from the ravaged colonies of Jupiter's moons, claim to have seen the hulk of an EDF42-Shield drifting in high orbit around the gas giant. Their stories agree on the essentials: the hull is torn open from end to end, the thrusters are dead, and the slow drift of the wreck is already tracing an unstable ellipse that will end by plunging it into the cloud bands. And yet the shield generator might still be salvageable — provided its core has not given way under the Avioids' fire.

We have to try to bring it back. A shield that still works, even damaged, would change the balance of power across the whole sector. The survivors speak of an intermittent flicker in the technical bay, a cold glow that still lights up in fits and starts, as if the system refused to die. No one has been able to get close enough to confirm it. The distress beacons fell silent weeks ago, and the last transmissions were nothing but noise.

The problem is that between us and the wreck lies a whole sector under Avioid control. Their patrols sweep the approach corridors, their orbital nests watch the Lagrange points, and the slightest propulsion signature beyond the debris line already draws a response. Reaching the hulk will take a precisely calculated trajectory, then an extraction under radio silence. If the generator holds, we will leave with it. If it has given way, we will only have confirmed the curse that weighs on the human race.
story_scene_sortie:
Mars burns its eternal red; down there, the NX01 lies dozing. From the Phobos bay, the sensors pick up tiny signatures, many of them, circling above the craters and weaving between the asteroid blocks. They are Avioids. Blue birds, the rare survivors say, because of the shade of their scaly skin, a slate blue, a night blue, and of the red glow smouldering in their eyes and in their chests.

No one knows what they are looking for. They do not communicate, they demand nothing. They patrol, they dive, they tear apart. With their wings of stretched leather, their white-hot talons and their plasma weapons, they have ripped apart more Shields than I have flying hours. They are the scouts of the horde, the fastest, the most numerous, and it always starts with them.

So never mind if the NX01 can barely stay in the air. You have to start somewhere. I will go out, face them one by one, and take a close look at what they are, because you only beat what you know well. If the quantum anchor does what Kamarasov promised, I will come back with enough to fill the first set of data. Otherwise… well, I will no longer have to worry about it.
story_scene_best2:
The blue ones are not alone. In the readings from the first sortie, other signatures keep coming back, denser, livelier, far from Mars, above a moon of Jupiter crushed by the striped mass of the giant. They are Avioids again. Khaki birds, the rare survivors say, because of the military green of their skin, an armour green, a dark moss green, and of the orange embers glowing in their eyes and deep in their chests.

Where the blue ones dive in a line, the khakis come in clusters and change course without warning. Their leather wings beat faster, their talons snap sooner, and their plasma shots come closer. They melt into the dust of destroyed stations. You do not see them coming, or else too late.

This time, I am not going out to look. I am going out to learn how to beat them. What lies behind those orange eyes, I will find out by watching them fall, one by one, and every page added to the Bestiary will make what comes next less perilous.
story_scene_best3:
The khakis are not the only ones on the prowl. Further out, in the rings of Saturn, the sensors pick up a signature I do not recognise. Heavier, slower, and strangely cold. These are no longer birds. The rare survivors speak of gargoyles, because of their dark metal carcass, bristling with plates, and of those red eyes that light up without a sound, deep inside a mask of stone and steel.

The blue ones dive in a line, the khakis come in clusters. The gargoyles form nothing at all. They drift alone between the blocks of ice, patient, then swoop on the first glow of an engine they come across. Their wings soak up shots like armour, and if you take too long to bring them down, they grow back. What the fire has torn away, the machine rebuilds.

So I will have to strike fast, and strike true. I know what I am risking, circling in their rings with a ship that can barely stay in the air. But every gargoyle that falls will fill one more page of the Bestiary, and teach me how to get the better of the next ones. If the quantum anchor does what Kamarasov promised, I will come back with what it takes to make them bend. Otherwise…
story_scene_best4:
The gargoyles are not the last. Far beyond Saturn, where the Sun is no more than one star among others, in front of the pale ice giant Uranus, the readings show more echoes, livelier, almost invisible. They are gargoyles again, but of a violet so deep it looks black, a violet that drinks the light and lets nothing of their carcass be seen. Only their red eyes give them away, two fixed embers closing in much faster than they should.

The survivors do not like to talk about them. Those who did say they hunt in packs, that they strike before you have even seen them, and that their wings, when they spread, swallow the very last glow of the ice giant. Some swear they grow back faster than the gargoyle. Others no longer swear by anything.

I do not know if the NX01 is made for this. But the Bestiary will only be worth something if it is complete, and it will not be as long as this page stays blank. So I am going, with fear in my gut and my finger on the trigger. If the quantum anchor keeps its promise, I will come back with what is missing. Otherwise, at least, I will not have had to tell the tale.
story_scene_bestboss:
There is one page of the Bestiary I have not dared to open. At the very end of known space, in orbit around Neptune, above blue storms that have been coiling on themselves for millions of years, the readings no longer show packs but a single echo, huge and motionless. A black saucer, cracked like old armour, ringed with red lights that pulse slowly. At the top of its dome, behind a dark bay, you can make out a tentacled creature that no one has approached and lived.

It is the one in command: the telepathic brain, the centre of the Avioids' collective intelligence. Gargoyles, green and dark, circle the saucer without ever straying from it. Hidden at its heart, behind the armour, it only shows itself when the way is clear, and then a single shot is enough. Just one. You still have to reach it. We have already brought one down. Another took its place, tougher, then another after that.

I do not know if a thing like that can truly be beaten. But each time it falls, I will be able to write one more line, and each line will make the next one less uncertain. So I am going. If the quantum anchor holds, I will tell it what I think of its breeding. Otherwise, it will be up to the next pilot to fill in the last page.
story_scene_paint_1:
Old Wallems' clandestine workshop, dug into the side of asteroid 434-Hungaria, is still running. Despite the invasion. Despite the patrols. You can still see hulls resting on trestles, open drums, masks bent over the metal…

I am not crazy enough to try to get through the hordes of Avioids that sweep the sector, row after row, just to have my ship repainted. No. I am not.

And yet the rumour holds. Wallems still takes orders, picks his unique shades by eye, and delivers magnificent hulls, all to a soundtrack of blazing trumpets…
No, I will not go, that would be madness…
story_scene_bar:
The airlock door hisses open, letting out a breath of recycled air that smells of coffee and rusty metal. I step onto the creaking floor of the Last Bulwark, the bar of Phobos station.

Around me is a rusty chaos of pink and blue neon flickering over vintage arcade cabinets. Cathode-ray screens hooked up to old game consoles sputter out scores in green pixels, while an old synthwave song crackles through the speakers.

I make my way between the tables. No one looks at me. Here, on the edge of the asteroid belt, everyone has a story, and no one asks questions.

It is the perfect place to forget that humanity is threatened with extinction.

I walk up to an arcade cabinet of Taito's *Phoenix*, in the darkest corner. A shiver runs down the back of my neck. On the black screen, a line of text blinks slowly:

FREE PLAY. PRESS SELECT(5) TO INSERT A CREDIT, THEN START(1) TO PLAY.

I follow the instructions.

And the game begins…
